newsitem.title: EGYPT: Excess Nile water spills into Egypt's desert.
newsitem.headline: Excess Nile water spills into Egypt's desert.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak watched the floodwaters of the Nile flow into the western desert on Tuesday and announced that work would start by January on a canal to irrigate 500,000 acres (200,000 hectares) of virgin land west of the Nile valley.

In a televised ceremony at Toshka on the western bank of Lake Nasser in the far south of Egypt, a dredger cleared away the sand which has been holding the water back since the lake reached record levels early this month.

Heavy rains in Ethiopia earlier this year have filled the lake to the brim and for the first time since the Aswan High Dam was built in the 1960s the Egyptians have had to divert some of it through the Toshka overflow canal.
The surface of the lake reached a record 178 metres (584 feet) above sea level earlier this month, enough to enter the canal, but workmen piled up sand to keep it back until Mubarak visited.

The Toshka canal will take the excess water 22 km (13 miles) into the Toshka depression west of Lake Nasser, where it will wait until the government finishes massive earth works to clear a passage north towards the oases of the New Valley.

The minister of public works and water resources, Abdel- Hadi Radi, told the ceremony the plan was to cut an irrigation canal 320 km (200 miles) long as far as the tiny desert settlement of Baris within five years at a cost of $1 billion and three billion pounds -- a total of $1.9 billion.
President Mubarak said the government would pay most of the costs as the project was too big for the private sector.
He named the canal after Sheikh Zaid al-Nahayan, the emir of Abu Dhabi and president of the United Arab Emirates, in recognition of the sheikh's aid to earlier irrigation projects.
"I believe he will play an effective role in building this canal because he also loves greenery and agriculture," he said.

Egyptian ministers portrayed the canal as a breakthrough in the country's many attempts to break out of the narrow confines of the Nile valley, where more than 90 percent of the 60 million Egyptians live on four percent of Egyptian territory.
The government has tried to attract people to new cities in the desert but most people are reluctant to move away from the greenery of the irrigated land.
Right on the other side of the country, the state is building a canal to take Nile water under the Suez Canal and irrigate 100,000 acres (40,000 hectares) in northern Sinai.
